Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
  • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
  • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun remarked. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office revealed earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over challenges from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he noted.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

In a recent development, china thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier stated he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

Industry observers note that china is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an key opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” noted Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

#116905. Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
  • Recent findings suggest that da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations.
  • Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Recent findings suggest that da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” claims Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Industry observers note that now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

Industry observers note that “Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” states Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”.

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

According to recent reports, but just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring latest hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation confirmed a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a fresh center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

It has been revealed that “Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” states Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

It has been revealed that “Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

In a recent development, but increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, notes Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” claims Murillo.

Sources indicate that to make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

According to recent reports, one manufacturer in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath claims it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

Industry observers note that one pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

Industry observers note that “It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

According to recent reports, cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he claims. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

#116904. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
  • Recent findings suggest that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024.
  • In a recent development, as of October 2026, data center developers have unveiled intends for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

Recent findings suggest that xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

In a recent development, as of October 2026, data center developers have unveiled intends for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence firm. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

In a recent development, building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a newly introduced industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Sources indicate that rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some vital questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” states Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Sources indicate that behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont indicates.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

Sources indicate that the on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.).

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi indicates. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

According to recent reports, bloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of unveiled projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, states Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi states. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

Sources indicate that while the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp states. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”.

In a recent development, looking to start up a board game night tradition? Well, Black Friday week is the perfect time to host the inaugural event, with price drops across all kinds of games — from family games to hardcore strategy brain-teasers — in Amazon's Black Friday sale.

Recent findings suggest that A board game isn't just the perfect thing to add to your arsenal of entertainment items at home. It's also a good gift idea for a hard-to-shop-for relative, older kids, or family who just doesn't want or need anything else — not to mention the potential for lots of fun with family and friends over Thanksgiving and Christmas.

Board games — or "table top gaming", to give it a proper name — is having a moment, which means there are lots of newly introduced and innovative titles available. There are twists on classics as well as ingenious new concepts. Don't worry if you're a bit lost in the gaming world, when it comes to board games we know our stuff, and we've combed the Black Friday listings to find you the best discounted games.

Industry observers note that here are the best Black Friday board game deals we've found so far. Keep checking back, however, as fresh deals will be added as Black Friday week rolls on.

There's a current trend for deception games, partly driven by the popularity of TV's The Traitors. Chameleon sees a group of players take turn to describe a word or concept without actually saying it. But one player is actually the Chameleon and has to guess the word from the other players' clues — all while avoiding detection. It's a ridiculous amount of fun, and perfect for major groups and players of all ages.

Catan is a veritable board game classic, and it's a great pick to snag while it's discounted. Three to four players settle a randomly laid-out island, collecting wood, brick, wool, grain, and ore to build roads, settlements, and cities. Games wrap up in about an hour to 90 minutes, and it's fairly easy to learn. And if you're tired of playing the same things over and over, Catan's modular board means no two games set up the same way. It's a significant upgrade from Monopoly that's suitable for the whole family.

The classics are classic for a reason. Mouse Trap has delighted kids and families for years, and nothing has changed after all this time. Indeed, it's as fiddly to set up as it ever was, but there's no denying the fun of setting the trap in motion. Kids will love the mechanics, parents will love the nostalgia. You can also find Black Friday discounts on other kids classics, including Connect 4, Battleship, and Candy Land.

Recent findings suggest that if you've ever wanted to get started with Dungeons & Dragons but didn't know how, this board game is the perfect introduction. It has a quick-start guide, player boards for the Cleric, Rogue, Wizard, and Fighter, and cards for species, backgrounds, spells, and gear so nobody has to build a character from scratch. Three to five players run through three adventure booklets split between combat, exploration, and roleplaying, and the poster maps for the Keep and the Caves of Chaos pull from one of the oldest modules in the game’s history. It's got everything beginners need and then some, so it's a much less daunting introductory experience.

If you haven't played the Horrified series, it's worth checking out for team-based beast-slaying. Players join forces to take on various classic monster — in this version it's American monsters that include Bigfoot, the Jersey Devil, and Mothman — with different ways of killing each monster. Board game fans will be familiar with the mechanics of the gameplay but the great thing about it is that you can mix and match the monsters, so each time you play is different. It can also get pretty tense as you ratchet up the difficulty level. Latest Update: Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
  • A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
  • The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office claims is completely false.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.

A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.

The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office claims is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.

The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.

Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.

But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.

Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.

The campaign has targeted Taiwan's President Lai (top) and his predecessor Tsai (bottom).

"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.

The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.

Sources indicate that more than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.

One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.

Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office remarked AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.

Many of the fake videos ridiculed President Lai and Shen while others portrayed other KMT candidates such as Ko Chih-en (above) in a positive light.

According to recent reports, other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.

In a recent development, A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.

Recent findings suggest that analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.

Sources indicate that the posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested indicated a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.

Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta noted it had removed the accounts.

According to recent reports, andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute stated the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.

"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests.".

Industry News: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).
  • It has been revealed that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration.
  • According to recent reports, the funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government (PDF).

It has been revealed that the list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”.

According to recent reports, the funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

Sources indicate that fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

It has been revealed that given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the new year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

Industry observers note that as part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission proposal that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test complications.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

Recent findings suggest that “Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”.

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a latest report.
  • Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.
  • Recent findings suggest that she found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a latest report.

Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.

Recent findings suggest that she found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.

Sources indicate that so Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor.".

Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.

Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report, external documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.

Sources indicate that spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.

North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.

"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," notes Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds.

Kim Bo-bin has been living in South Korea for 15 years now.

First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.

Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.

In a recent development, three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.

According to recent reports, pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.

Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.

An image from 2010 showing the inside of a state-sanctioned church in Pyongyang.

This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.

Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East.".

Industry observers note that rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.

The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant claims she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".

North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.

All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt states.

And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.

North Koreans pay tribute to statues of the late Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il.

Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.

Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.

Recent findings suggest that one of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.

Recent findings suggest that when a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.

Industry observers note that kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.

It has been revealed that while picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.

A view of the city of Chongjin in North Korea's North Hamgyong province.

Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.

According to recent reports, kim Bo-bin states it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.

Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them.

Sources indicate that in her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?".

Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps.

It has been revealed that lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, states she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory.

Lee Young-joo first met a Christian after she escaped from North Korea into China.

She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC.

According to recent reports, kim indicates she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God.".

Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later.

Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied.

Industry observers note that today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told.

It has been revealed that kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

Could Kim's teen daughter become North Korea's next leader?

Kim Jong Un was meant to be their only idol - then North Koreans discovered K-pop.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.
  • Recent findings suggest that "I have long had three goals," he mentioned.
  • Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Max Calce made the surprise announcement that he would be moving to the Brantford Bulldogs of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) in a statement issued on the website of his German Ice Hockey League (DEL) team, Adler Mannheim late on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that "I have long had three goals," he mentioned. "To play for the Adler, in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), and in the NHL. Today is a difficult and emotional day for me, as I say goodbye to my home.".

Having started the season in Mannheim, many thought the 17-year-old would finish the season in the DEL.

The announcement came after Calce, who had been a regular in Mannheim's lineup this season, had been left off the team sheet for Tuesday night's game in Straubing.

This comes less than a month after he became the youngest-ever player to score a goal for the German men's national team – against Slovakia in Germany's final game of the annual Deutschland Cup invitational.

"It was only a matter of time; he's an incredible player," remarked former NHL player Tobias Rieder, who frequently played on a line with Calce during the tournament.

"The most impressive thing is that, at 17, he plays a very mature style of hockey—he almost always makes the right decision.".

Calce is also the youngest goal scorer in DEL history, having found the net for Mannheim in September 2025 at just 16 years and 100 days old.

In his statement, the centerman thanked Mannheim, which has produced a number of NHL players over the years, including Leon Draisaitl, Moritz Seider and Tim Stützle.

"The trust, support, and experiences I gained through my coaches, teammates, and everyone within the organization have played a major role in my development—both as a player and as a person.".

This season, his second in the DEL, Calce has six goals and two assists in Mannheim's first 19 games.

"We believe in preparing young players to take opportunities at the highest level of the sport," Dallas Eakins, Mannheim's head coach and sporting director stated.

"As much as we would have loved to continue to have him play for us, we respect and welcome his ambition.".

On the surface, the notion of moving from a men's professional league to a junior league may seem like a step backwards, but Calce's move to the OHL will give Calce increased exposure to NHL scouts. The OHL is one of the top three junior leagues in Canada and according to figures released by the CHL last season, they produce more NHL players than any other developmental system.

In doing so, Calce is now following the path of Edmonton Oilers superstar Draisaitl, who left Mannheim's youth program at the age of 16 to pursue his NHL dream, joining the Western Hockey League's Prince Albert Raiders.

According to recent reports, this, of course is not the only path to the NHL; Moritz Seider of the Detroit Red Wings and the Ottawa Senators' Tim Stützle were both first-round draft choices plucked directly from Mannheim. Calce is hoping to be taken in the first round of next summer's NHL Entry Draft.

Born to Russian parents in Mannheim, Calce changed his birth surname, Penkin, to that of his mother and stepfather last summer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it occurs to me that, as a new(ish) father, and someone who reviews products for a living, I am a nightmare to get gifts for. I’m not alone. Most of my friends have no idea what to get their dad, and end up brainstorming in group chats with anyone they can get their hands on.

Recent findings suggest that fear not, I’m here to make gifting a little easier this year (or at the very least, contribute to the brainstorm). Below are some of the best WIRED-tested gifts for the dad or father figure in your life, including travel gadgets, dad-approved apparel, and best-in-class earbuds. I’ve personally gifted a few of these to my dad, with great results.

Updated November 2026: I swapped and added a few newly introduced picks, including watches and apparel.

Recent findings suggest that another classic gift I’ve seen win over not just Dad, but everyone else in the room, too (everyone wanted a turn). This massage gun has the signature Theragun triangle grip, which makes it far easier to target hard-to-reach places compared to other brands that have a straight grip. It comes with three ball head attachments (standard, dampener, and thumb), and lasts up to 120 minutes on a single charge.

These are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. That’s why I love them for outdoor runs and bike rides. This premium model uses a mix of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that’s clearer than most smaller open earbuds. You can learn more in our full Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 review.

Industry observers note that this Garmin watch is just right for the dad who is getting really into running and wants to dig into more advanced metrics and detailed training aims than what’s offered on most smartwatches. Like any good fitness tracker, the Forerunner 165 has superb battery life (up to 11 days), a colorful touchscreen, and plenty of buttons that make it easy to control with gloved or sweaty hands. It’s also one of the brand’s most affordable running watches. You can learn more in our full Garmin Forerunner 165 review.

It has been revealed that I can’t think of many dads who don’t love an electric bike. The Letric XP4 750 isn’t just one of WIRED’s top electric bike picks, it’s one of the best-selling electric vehicles in America, ranking third behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 in 2024. WIRED reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani states it only took 20 minutes to assemble and lasted well over 50 miles of riding on a single charge. This version has an upgraded 750-watt motor that helps tackle hillier terrain than the original.

Recent findings suggest that this is my favorite power bank, full stop. If I am traveling, going abroad, camping, or just headed to work, I take this power bank. It’s the built-in, retractable USB-C cord that does it for me—it’s there when you need it, and out of the way when you don’t. It’s small enough to pack in any bag and light enough that I barely notice it. Plus, it has an extra USB-A and USB-C port built in, so you can charge multiple devices at once if you want.

In a recent development, I’ve lost count of how many times my Apple AirTag Bluetooth tracker has saved me from the hassle of looking for something. Keys: located. Luggage: tracked. Backpack: safe and sound. Sure, it’s not the most exciting gift in the world, but it’s the epitome of useful and practical. As long as they use an iPhone, that is.

It has been revealed that “If you told me I could only have one bag in my life, the 26L version of the GoRuck GR1 would be my pick,” says WIRED operations manager and outdoor expert Scott Gilbertson (he’s also a dad). It’s absolutely in buy-it-for-life territory, built with ultra-durable, water-resistant 1000D Cordura and tested by US Army Special Forces. It’s technically made for rucking, but it can do basically anything you throw at it, travel included. This Huckberry version omits the exterior MOLLE webbing, giving it a sleeker look. You can read more in Gilbertson’s full GoRuck GR1 review.

It has been revealed that the best aluminum carry-on suitcase. Aluminum luggage is sleek and durable, with a shell that just looks better with little dents and dings (unlike polycarbonate luggage). Aluminum itself is recyclable and repairable, and the clamps that hold the Rimowa together won’t fail or break as easily as your typical zipper. Rimowa is obviously the “it” brand for this type of luggage, but you can get similar options from Away and Level8 for well under half the price.

A reusable water bottle is something I thought I only needed one of. Turns out, the more the merrier. I now have four and have realized there’s a good place for each one (in my case, one for the house, one for my work bag, and one for the nightstand). The Owala FreeSip has been my favorite for years, usurping my Hydro Flask and S’well for water bottle supremacy. Plus it comes in literally dozens of colors—there’s definitely one he’ll love.

It’s one of the simplest ways to take pictures without getting distracted by your phone or overwhelmed by mirrorless camera settings to fiddle with. This latest model adds desperately needed updates like a button to toggle between filters and a faster shutter button. According to recent reports, if Dad loves to host large get-togethers, parties, or tailgates, this portable party speaker is one of the loudest, most durable I’ve tested. Amazon (with Wireless Charging Case).

If Dad loves his music, podcasts, and TV demonstrates, no matter where he is, these will be a trusty companion for his next adventure, whether that’s on the couch or on his next long-haul flight.

This is one of the brand's portable samplers, sequencers, and composers that Dad can make music on, wherever he is. Despite its small size, it has ample pads and dials, a built-in microphone and line input for audio recording, 64GB of internal memory, and 999 sample slots.

Industry observers note that I basically lived in one of these tees during parental leave. It’s absolutely the softest tee I own, with a fabric that never bothered my sensitive skin. It’s athletic without being too slim-fitting, stretchy without feeling cheap, and a great do-everything (or do nothing on the couch) tee for anyone, not just Dad.

In a recent development, another do-everything piece of apparel, but decidedly more technical than the Vuori tee. These are my go-to pants for walks, hikes, and camping trips. They are very lightweight and have a reasonably athletic fit, water-repellent finish, adjustable drawstring waist, and durable ripstop polyester I’ve yet to poke a hole through.

The gift that never fails. I’ve seen the Brooks Ghost gifted to me, my dad, my father-in-law, and others. No one has ever looked disappointed. These are great running shoes for just about anyone, with neutral support and plenty of cushion. I’ve used the 18s (and previous 17s, 16s, 15s) for dozens of miles of walking and running this year—they are comfortable and reliable. Plus, you are supposed to replace your running shoes every six months or so, which I’m sure your dad has not done.

Sources indicate that dads who run need more running shirts. I certainly do. This Ten Thousand Session Shirt is one of my go-tos because it is breathable enough for a serious run, but looks normal enough to go to the café afterward. It’s made from 100 percent polyester—no nylon or spandex to be found here, which means it dries fast and absorbs very little water, in my experience.

Recent findings suggest that sneakers in the office are going extinct—haven’t you heard? WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman noticed these on GQ editor Jordan Bowman, and we have to pass along the loafer recommendation because the “buttery smooth” leather alone is worth a small splurge.

In a recent development, the best merino wool socks, period. They are antimicrobial and wick sweat, but also keep your feet dry and keep them thermoregulated. Plus the brand has a lifetime warranty on these socks—if you ever get a hole, send them back for a replacement pair (we did).

This Benrus diver is the rare tool watch you can dress up, thanks to its elegant size and vintage style. It's 20 percent off right now; WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman ordered one to test out in December.

Industry observers note that …Or spend one tenth the cost of the Benrus for an indestructible Dad watch. Inspired by the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, this Casio reveals great design and good taste doesn't need to cost thousands.

In a recent development, A headlamp is an infinitely useful outdoor tool—you can use it for camping; yard work (early or late in the day); home maintenance; or, if you’re my dad, grilling after the sun has set. If he loves ultralight, this is the cup for him. If he has no idea what ultralight is but wants a super lightweight cup for drinks or snacks around the house, this too is a fun option. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested all kinds of jump starters on his old Land Cruiser, and recommends this one as the best compact option. Like all of the brand’s appliances, it’s easy to use, so it's more fun than work to make that fan-favorite pizza just right.

Cometeer (World Mug Collection).

In a recent development, when my son was born last year, I lost the time to grind and brew, so I found myself stocking my fridge with disappointingly bitter bulk-bottled iced coffee (or spending $7 on a café cold brew). My wife got us a coffee subscription to Cometeer, which flash-freezes freshly ground small-batch coffee and ships them in recyclable pods—just add water, hot or cold, to dial in the strength. You can take the time to mix and match roasters each month or just set your faves and forget it. After six months of testing, I can safely say I haven’t had a bad cup. I miss the aromatics I get and comfort I feel from a truly fresh grind, but each pour feels like a tiny treat, even at 5 am. It’s a whole little moment: My 16-month-old chugs his bottle while I stir up oat milk, ice, and Counter Culture. He’s learning to say “cheers.” I look forward to those early mornings a bit more than I used to. —Cooper Fleishman.

Industry observers note that if they love a cocktail, this toolkit from Umami Mart elevates the mixing experience to something more refined. Umami Mart is an independently owned small business in Oakland that’s part sake bar, part sake class space, and part online barware store. This kit includes a diamond-cut mixing glass, julep strainer, stainless steel jigger, and stainless steel teardrop barspoon, all made in Japan and sourced by the brand.

The Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

Tossing a Frisbee around is part fun, part an excuse to hang out and talk. It’s a classic dads-and-kids activity that lasts for years, even as interests and hobbies change. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar says that, over time, the ask to toss the Frisbee around shifts from the kid to the adult. Either way, the Aerobie is one of the best flying discs you can buy.

It has a fully digital smart display that lets you select between shooting styles and shows you how much ammo you have left. It refills much faster than the SpyraThree (20 shots in about 12 seconds). It’s recommended for kids (and adults) 14 and up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Car buyers in Newly introduced York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year.
  • “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car.
  • Industry observers note that in the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Car buyers in Newly introduced York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

“People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in Latest York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor said.

Industry observers note that in the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

It has been revealed that we end people might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car tech giant—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

Some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board stated that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”.

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the latest law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

It has been revealed that A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the fresh rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.
