📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the firm's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he stated during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump â potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal â one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy â the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Recent findings suggest that was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has noted that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any fresh revelations could further damage the manufacturer's standing â and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he remarked.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away.

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump.

US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation.

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO.

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang â noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" â could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors.".

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI â which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" â will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the firm at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble â like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 â that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

Sources indicate that on Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

#116888. AI is straining America’s open records systems

AI is straining America’s open records systems

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all.
  • Panton used to get a request every year or so from a firm called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper.
  • Recent findings suggest that rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a firm called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”.

Recent findings suggest that rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

Industry observers note that at the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

According to recent reports, the US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

In a recent development, this is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”.

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

Sources indicate that smartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” notes Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the firm has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich states Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”.

Recent findings suggest that while incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

Sources indicate that but the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

Industry observers note that in small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, Newly introduced York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our latest normal is high,” she claims. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

Industry observers note that it’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a Upcoming York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

It has been revealed that in Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button matter, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

According to recent reports, while more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

In a recent development, on the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus states its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”.

Sources indicate that as volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies upcoming ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she notes, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”.

Sources indicate that arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

In a recent development, neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich indicates the upcoming rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”.

Industry observers note that fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” notes Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Recent findings suggest that startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

Industry observers note that as states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” claims Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source stated, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person stated, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source stated, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person stated, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have mentioned.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it claims is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

Recent findings suggest that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

According to recent reports, the balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official mentioned in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Recent findings suggest that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, noted at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

Recent findings suggest that the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Industry observers note that still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

#116880. Latest Update: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

Latest Update: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV.
  • According to recent reports, so, for the manufacturer’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

According to recent reports, so, for the manufacturer’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to fresh heights of power and performance.

That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

For Porsche’s newly introduced Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

According to recent reports, porsche isn’t saying how substantial the fresh roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

The upcoming Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

In a recent development, but it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

You can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

This car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

That’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

Recent findings suggest that to bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

Sources indicate that what they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The new 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

According to recent reports, enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

In a recent development, lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

Sources indicate that this whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

In a recent development, don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

Cruising is better in the new 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without issue.

It has been revealed that and it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly substantial enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

In a recent development, so, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

#116877. Tidal is banning AI-generated music entirely

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (461 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Tidal is banning AI-generated music entirely

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (461 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tidal will soon become the first streaming service to take a decisive stance against AI-generated music.
  • The move comes after Tidal confirmed earlier this year it would demonetize all fully AI-generated track, and label every such song as either AI-generated or AI-assisted.
  • A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The company expects to purge 29 million tracks.

Tidal will soon become the first streaming service to take a decisive stance against AI-generated music. On Tuesday, the firm revealed it would begin removing wholly genAI tracks from its catalog come December 9. According to platform lead Robert Anderson, Tidal's decision will result in the deletion of approximately 29 million tracks, and set the service on the path to reject 80,000 to 85,000 songs daily. "We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96 percent of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all," Anderson wrote on X. "We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit.".

The move comes after Tidal confirmed earlier this year it would demonetize all fully AI-generated track, and label every such song as either AI-generated or AI-assisted. On Tuesday, however, Anderson mentioned even that policy hasn't been enough to combat the deluge of AI tracks that has been flooding Tidal in recent months. Over the last 90 days, 43 percent of all tracks uploaded to the service were flagged as AI-generated, according to the tech giant.

A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that's enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done...

According to recent reports, that Tidal should be the first streaming service to ban AI content is somewhat surprising. Block, the company that has owned Tidal since 2021, is led by AI enthusiast Jack Dorsey. At the start of the year, Block made headlines when it laid off 4,000 of its 10,000 employees, with Dorsey attributing the decision entirely to AI. "The core thesis is simple. Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company," he wrote at the time. "A significantly smaller team, using the tools we're building, can do more and do it better.".

It has been revealed that the only other streaming platform besides Tidal to outright ban music "generated wholly or in substantial part by AI" is Bandcamp. Spotify, for instance, has tried to dance around the problem; in October, the company said it would continue to remove "slop and spam" from people's recommendations, but it did this shortly after announcing it would also allow people to remix and cover songs using AI. Soundcloud got into bed with AI music creation companies Elevenlabs and Moises; its current policies try to balance the removal of spam with allowing AI tools to proliferate. Deezer added a toggle to hide (but not delete) AI-made music, while Apple Music merely labels songs made with AI.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?

#116874. Natalie Tran is turning short-form comedy into a filmmaking career

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2634 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Natalie Tran is turning short-form comedy into a filmmaking career

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.
  • Recent findings suggest that she started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films.
  • Recent findings suggest that then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Tran had already spent most of her life performing by the time one of her videos unexpectedly took off online.

Recent findings suggest that she started acting at five, first through musical theater and later through commercials and indie films. Content creation came much later — initially as something she did for fun, not as an attempt to build an audience.

Recent findings suggest that then, at the end of 2023, one of her videos went viral. "I was gaining so many followers, I couldn't even believe it," Tran told Mashable at VidCon 2026.

According to recent reports, but going viral was only the beginning. Tran took the comedic persona and format that audiences responded to and kept building, eventually turning short-form sketches into another arm of a career that still revolves around her original love: acting. Now she's trying to bring those worlds even closer together.

According to recent reports, tran recently wrapped Passion Project, a roughly 17-minute short film she wrote, directed, produced, and acted in, with hopes of using it as a proof of concept for a future feature. And rather than seeing her years making social video as separate from filmmaking, she claims the skills she developed online — from finding the hook to obsessing over an edit — made directing feel surprisingly familiar.

"It feels like one of my skits, just higher budget," she remarked.

For Mashable's Creator Playbook, Tran talks about what happens after a viral moment, why short-form comedy taught her to be a better filmmaker, the changing relationship between creators and Hollywood, and why sometimes ambition just has to be louder than insecurity.

In a recent development, mashable: You started acting when you were five. How did content creation eventually enter the picture?

Natalie Tran: I auditioned for a play called The King and I because I'd always been singing. That's actually where I started — as a singer. Surprisingly, I'm mainly an actor now, but I thought I was going to be a singer initially.

I got into musical theater and, from there, moved on to commercial work, indie films, all that jazz. That's what led me into content creation because I really like performing. I like making funny videos, things like that. I'd been making videos here and there, but never to get an audience, just kind of for fun.

Sources indicate that at the very tail end of 2023, I made a video that went viral. It blew up, and then I kind of took the bit and ran with it. Now I'm here. It's been interesting to see how acting and content creation can work together. Every day I'm kind of building that brand and making it work.

Anyone can have a viral video. What did you do after yours took off to turn that moment into something bigger?

At first, I was just shocked. I was like, "There's no way this is happening." I was gaining so many followers; I couldn't even believe it. Then I started making videos. My favorite thing ever is when people comment that I'm funny. I love being called funny. It's my favorite compliment. That made me really happy to be recognized for that because I'm actually a pretty shy person. I like that I'm now recognized for my personality.

I think I can show my personality not just through my videos, but also when I direct something, make movies, or do long-form work. It's also helped me become a more sociable person in general. Everything kind of works together to build my career.

Your comedy works really well in short-form. Do you think those skills translate to long-form filmmaking?

Definitely. I just wrapped a short film, and that'll be about 17 minutes. The goal is for that to be a proof of concept for feature films in the future.

In a recent development, I think short-form has really helped me because, you know, how in school there's always a word count? They're like, "Get below the word count." You can get the idea faster. With short-form, it's: Get the audience hooked in the first three seconds. I think that still applies to long-form because you want to make it engaging.

Now that I have this short-form experience, I can kind of be like, "OK, this can be a bunch of different short ideas that I can stitch together." That's kind of how I think about it now.

How much intention goes into those first three seconds?

Recent findings suggest that when I make a video, I make sure my face is the first thing they see. I think about high energy right away. Maybe not the best joke — you want to keep the punchline for the end — but you want to have something really engaging.

Industry observers note that you think of an idea and then ask, "OK, what can make it even funnier? What's going to make someone stop scrolling and be like, 'Oh, I want to watch this whole video?'" Sometimes it sucks because it's like, "I don't want to have to make the first thing a clickbait reaction." So it's a matter of thinking about what's worth it.

It has been revealed that there's a balance. You don't want to draw your audience in and then have the rest of the video be something they didn't actually want to watch.

Why do you think comedy works so well in short-form?

Sources indicate that the biggest thing about comedy is timing, and that's really key with shorts. It's like boom, boom, boom. I'm a very percussive comedian, I would say. I'm so picky with the edit.

In a recent development, it depends because I also love comedy that's dry — no edit, literally nothing. But then I also love the comedy where it's cut, cut, cut, cut, cut. That's why it does so well in short-form. With these short attention spans, it works because it keeps you engaged the whole time.

Tell me about Passion Project. What made you finally decide to write and direct something yourself?

Sources indicate that I've been acting since I was young, and people would ask me a lot, "Do you ever want to write or direct something?" And I would think, "Yeah, yeah, yeah." Then I was in a feature film last year called Frogman Returns, and I was really drawn to the way it was shot. It was a lot of one-ers, and I saw the way the actor chemistry worked on camera.

Sources indicate that it was generating ideas, so I came up with the idea of Passion Project on that set. It was very early stages, but I remember I still have the voice memo where I was like, "Oh my gosh, it could be this thing where it's a lot of one-ers and really good actors.".

Acting is the main thing. That's my love. I sat on it for half a year. Then over winter break, my friend was at a party, and she mentioned, "Natalie, someone has the same idea as you." And I went, "Nope. That's not gonna happen. I'm making it.".

It has been revealed that that was the kick in the butt I needed to start writing it. It was about five months of pre-production and rewrites, and then we shot it in May. It was a dream come true. I'd been on camera a lot and worked as an actor my whole life, but this was my first time really being the producer, director, and writer behind everything. I found that I really love it.

How did being a content creator prepare you to direct a film?

I asked in my producing class one day, "Have you ever had a director who is also an actor in it?" Because everyone wants to say that it's very hard to direct and act in your own movie. I disagree.

According to recent reports, the reason is because I have all this content creation experience where I'm filming with a friend, I ask them to record me, I watch the playback, I go, "OK, redo it. Change the angle. I'm gonna change my acting." And that's exactly how it was on set. I kept telling everyone, "This feels like one of my skits, just higher budget.".

It has been revealed that content creation helped me so much because I already had that acting background, but filming my skits and finding out what I like in my own videos really helped me. Now I know how to communicate that to a team.

Recent findings suggest that there used to be this idea that creators used the internet as a stepping stone to Hollywood. Does that distinction still feel relevant to you?

I think it's a lot easier now. I think it's the time where creators are bursting out of their bubble. Before, it was hard to get discovered. I'm lucky because I did have the traditional acting background, but now that I'm able to put my own stuff out there, it's an extra push.

Because of that, I'm able to put myself out there. I've gotten with a great agency and management, and all these things have been helping me build my career.

It's a really interesting time. I feel like a lot of people didn't expect it to be this way. It's growing every day, and more people are talking about creators getting into Hollywood.

According to recent reports, social following is even becoming part of traditional casting now. How have you seen those worlds collide?

According to recent reports, I'll get auditions now, and sometimes they'll ask for your socials. I just think that's interesting, how it's a factor now. It's hit-or-miss because you don't want to cast people solely for their following, of course.

Recent findings suggest that with Passion Project, I purposely sought out creators who are actors but also do content because that's where I come from. It was really fun to have that room of people who had the same understanding of this industry. People recognize the faces in the movie, but I'm not just hiring any Joe Schmo off the internet. I had a casting process as well. It's interesting to see how those worlds collide.

Industry observers note that acting and content creation used to feel like two separate sides of your career. Do they still?

When I started social media, it was almost a battle. If you even look at my Instagram feed, I had my pictures and it was all acting, modeling, acting, modeling. Then you swipe over and it's me being like — what is this weird juxtaposition?

According to recent reports, before, it was kind of battling with each other. Now I'm learning to marry the two and really have them work together.

Authenticity gets talked about constantly in creator spaces. How do you stay authentic when so much of your content is satirical?

According to recent reports, I blew up kind of for satirical videos, and a lot of people got it. They were like, "Oh, I know you're not actually like that." And then some people thought I was like that, and I'm like, "Wait, but now I'm not being authentic." It's hard. I consider myself pretty multifaceted. I'll livestream, and I never really like to play characters in my livestream. I'll do accents all the time — I love to do an accent — but I'm not gonna fake stuff.

That's where my authenticity comes from. I'm always gonna be real. Someone asks me a question, I'll answer real. I'm not gonna give you a fake answer. It can get difficult with content because you do want to play things up sometimes for the video. But luckily, since I come from the sketch comedy world, it's always going to be a bit. You can tell it's not real.

What do you think keeps people coming back to your content?

I think it's how weird I am. I talk in accents all the time. My manager literally went, "Who is this?" It's just fun. I like putting on silly voices and making weird faces and just being myself on camera. But it's also funny because when people meet me in real life, they're like, "Oh, you're way more chill." It comes out in bursts. I think that's what makes my videos fun.

What's your advice for someone who's scared to put themselves out there?

Just put yourself out there. If you are confident in what you do, just do it. Don't care about what other people think. And I'm saying that, and I do care about what other people think. I get scared to post things sometimes because I'm scared of people thinking it's stupid or commenting something mean.

But luckily, I think my drive is higher than my insecurity. I don't know what to call it. Put yourself out there, because if you're passionate about what you do — I've used the word passion over and over again, especially because of Passion Project — it's gonna pay off. If you love what you do, it's worth it to pursue it.

Do you still read the comments?

Sources indicate that when I first blew up, I would read every single comment. Even on the video that I always talk about that blew me up — I think that one got over 20 million views — I think I literally read every comment. I was on my phone because it's a dopamine rush. It's honestly pretty shocking initially.

Now I've gotten to the point where once in a while I'll check my DMs or look at the comments. It depends on my mood. There are some videos where maybe I've read every comment. There are some videos where I don't think I even opened the comment section. I'm kind of sporadic.

Do those metrics mean less to you now than they used to?

Sources indicate that yes. I think I'm more prone to looking at the comments on videos that I'm really proud of because those are always really nice. But there are some videos — and I don't make these as much anymore — that were a little more rage bait. A lot of the comments were mean, and so I take one look, and I'm like, "Never mind. I'm done.".

It has been revealed that there are days when I'll open my comment section, and it ruins my day. That'll happen. That's another piece of advice to creators. I'm one to say it because I do let it ruin my day sometimes, but try not to. That's all you can do.

So: have fun, put yourself out there, don't get consumed by the comments or views, and maybe do a funny little accent.

Do a funny little accent. Everyone will love it.

It has been revealed that crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. Her work focuses on the people, platforms, and communities shaping modern entertainment, from YouTube creators and livestreamers to fandoms, social media trends, and the evolving relationship between technology and culture. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

Recent findings suggest that previously, she was the entertainment director at MTV News, where she helped expand the brand's coverage of fan culture, K-pop, and the internet's most passionate communities. Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

She's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.
  • He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage.
  • In a recent development, this is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”.

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

In a recent development, this is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Major Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”.

Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a newly introduced toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.).

It has been revealed that as it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

Sources indicate that what started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”.

Industry observers note that the videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”.

Industry observers note that meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he notes. “So I got a kick out of it.”.

According to recent reports, meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their highlights.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Massive Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”).

Industry observers note that though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Major Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he claims.

Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.).

It has been revealed that “This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”.

Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.).

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”.

In a recent development, essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of upcoming, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he states. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”.

Ways you can help your video doorbell stay charged in the winter

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter can be tough on battery-powered video doorbells, but a few adjustments may help yours cope when temperatures drop.
  • Recent findings suggest that while video doorbells aren't a necessity per se, it can be hard to imagine living without them once you own one.
  • It has been revealed that another catch is that they're perpetually outdoors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter can be tough on battery-powered video doorbells, but a few adjustments may help yours cope when temperatures drop.

Recent findings suggest that while video doorbells aren't a necessity per se, it can be hard to imagine living without them once you own one. Knowing who's at the door saves you run-ins with unwanted salesmen. More seriously, they may help deter burglars — or help you catch an offender in the act if deterrence fails. Of course, your ability to capture that activity will depend in part on the distance at which your video doorbell stops detecting motion.

It has been revealed that another catch is that they're perpetually outdoors. That might not be such a major deal if you live somewhere warm like Miami or San Antonio. But in places with prolonged cold weather, battery life can suffer to the point that a video doorbell becomes more of a burden than an aid. It's inherent to the chemistry of lithium-ion technology, unfortunately.

According to recent reports, the main way to alleviate this issue is by bringing your doorbell or its battery in from the cold. There may be other tactics you can employ, though, such as strategic positioning.

In a recent development, the critical point here is that an ideal charging range for lithium-ion batteries is between 50 and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (10 to 30 Celsius). When charging below the freezing point, there's a risk that metallic lithium will start plating onto electrodes, permanently reducing capacity. And even if the weather is slightly above freezing, charging will be less efficient than it could be. Cold-weather performance is one of the differences between sodium and lithium-ion batteries.

Before you charge a doorbell battery, make sure to let it warm up to room temperature first. This should not only preserve capacity but also help avoid cold-related charging delays. That's significant, considering that a Ring battery can take as long as 10 hours to top up. Let the battery charge fully before putting it back outside to maximize the time between recharges. If your doorbell has a removable battery, keeping a charged spare will minimize downtime. Some models in Ring's updated battery-powered doorbell lineup feature quick-release battery packs to make swaps easier.

Sources indicate that some doorbells don't offer removable batteries, however. One example is the battery-powered Google Nest Doorbell. In that case, you'll need to become familiar with removing your doorbell and bringing it indoors. Be sure to time this properly. Since a recharge might take several hours, it's probably wise to charge overnight unless you're worried about security and don't have any other cameras covering the front of your home.

Sources indicate that in climates with borderline winters — that is, where the temperature only occasionally dips below freezing — you may be able to extend battery life by aiming or sheltering your doorbell in just the right way. If you can block the wind, for example, or maximize sunlight, your doorbell will naturally run warmer than it might otherwise.

Industry observers note that A vital point here is that in extreme cold, it's possible for a doorbell to stop functioning for the duration. Anker, Ring, Google and others all agree on a minimum operating temperature of -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 Celsius). Between that and the freezing point, devices may still refuse to charge in order to prevent the plating we mentioned earlier.

Honestly, then, the best choice if you live in a frostbitten region may be to switch to a wired doorbell, as long as you can find one compatible with your home's design. While wired doorbells may still encounter problems around the -4 degrees Fahrenheit mark, they're otherwise immune to the cold, since they draw on the same electricity as the rest of your house.

Tech Report: Tidal unveils ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them.
  • Recent findings suggest that tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI.
  • It has been revealed that as things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the firm is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.

Recent findings suggest that tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

It has been revealed that as things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.

Credit: Tidal Credit: Tidal.

Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an glitch with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal states it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.

Recent findings suggest that as of December 9, individual uploaders and distributors will no longer be allowed to add AI music to Tidal. However, they could lie, couldn’t they?

Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects AI music, but it will probably rely on watermarking. Almost every AI song on Tidal (94 percent) comes from Suno, which added watermarking earlier this year. Tidal also cites Google Lyria as a source of AI tunes, which has SynthID labels embedded in the waveform. Deezer claimed it has a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate of less than 0.01 percent, but it’s unclear if Tidal is using that or something similar.

That will take care of most AI music, but this approach won’t detect everything. There are open models for music generation that you can run locally on a GPU, and some cloud-based providers aren’t bothering to watermark their outputs. Even if Tidal is using a separate detection system, fresh models may be able to evade it—it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game. This will be a problem with verifying provenance in all types of media in the future. For the time being, at least, Tidal’s policy should clear out most of the AI slop.

Recent findings suggest that the people directing robots to make these songs will have plenty of other options after Tidal blocks AI. Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer, and Apple Music all allow AI music on their platforms with labeling. Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks from its collection based on user feedback. Other streamers haven’t specified how much slop (if any) they’ve cleared out.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
  • "Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound ​impact on our societies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.

The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.

"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound ​impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen mentioned in a statement.

"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point.".

Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The upcoming rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.

The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.

Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.

While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.

By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.

Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.

Sources indicate that around one-third of the world's quantum companies ⁠are ​based in the European Union, according to ​the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.

However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.

The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.

The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.

The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You no longer need to free up 212GB on your PS5 for Rockstar’s blockbuster.
  • The PlayStation Store page for the game now states that "PS5 and PS Portal cloud streaming [is] supported only with Premium subscription." I bought GTA 6 on a separate account from the one that my PS Plus subscription is on, so I haven't been able to test it yet, unfortunately.
  • A report last month suggested Xbox would have exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You no longer need to free up 212GB on your PS5 for Rockstar’s blockbuster.

The PlayStation Store page for the game now states that "PS5 and PS Portal cloud streaming [is] supported only with Premium subscription." I bought GTA 6 on a separate account from the one that my PS Plus subscription is on, so I haven't been able to test it yet, unfortunately.

A report last month suggested Xbox would have exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6. However, Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball clarified that wasn't the case.

It has been revealed that much like with Xbox Cloud Gaming, it doesn't seem that there's a way for PlayStation users to stream their copy of GTA 6 to PC via the cloud. Remote play from your console to PC still works (I forgot about that option and it's about to destroy my productivity).

The maker of Asobi, a third-party app that supported PS Plus Premium streaming, mentioned last week Sony was blocking its connections to stream PS5 games from the service. Cloud versions of PS3 and PS4 titles and remote play from a PS5 console still work on Asobi. Sony is also shutting down its own PlayStation Plus app for PC next month because barely anyone was using it, but that's mainly for PS3 and PS4 games anyway.

It's perhaps worth noting that PS Plus Premium will stream GTA 6 at PS5 quality. The Xbox Cloud Gaming streams are limited to Xbox Series S graphics settings. Xbox Cloud Gaming also has time limits as of this month, while PS Plus Premium does not.

Sources indicate that sony revealed on Monday that GTA 6 was the biggest game release in the platform's history. More than 39 million unique players explored Leonida on PS5 on the game's first weekend, logging 683 million hours of total gameplay. Developer Rockstar Games remarked it sold 32.5 million pre-orders of GTA 6, generating $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales.

Sources indicate that A PC version of GTA 6 is all but certainly on the way, perhaps as soon as early next year. Efforts are underway to recompile the leaked Xbox build for PC as well.
