Blade Runner 2099 finally takes this franchise to the stars

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories.
  • It has been revealed that like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts.
  • In a recent development, this is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories. However, there's one area where the TV show completely outpaces both films.

It has been revealed that like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts. Its world is one of bustling streets, crowded apartment buildings, and the massive pyramids that tower over the Los Angeles skyline. Yet episode 2 opens with a different landscape entirely: a fiery red terrain bursting with rocky crags and rushing lava flows.

In a recent development, this is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea. It's also the first time an on-screen Blade Runner project has been to space. (Notably, comic Blade Runner 2019: Off World has already blasted off to space.).

It has been revealed that space travel is a fact of life in the world of Blade Runner, as well as in its source material, Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? As part of larger space colonization attempts, humans are moving to off-world settlements. Who is preparing these settlements for human occupation? Replicants (or androids in the novel), whose enhanced strength and durability make them the ideal slave labor force for braving inhospitable outer space environments.

According to recent reports, while off-world colonies seem prime for sci-fi exploration, they have just been a background world-building detail in the Blade Runner franchise. Billboards frequently tease the promise of a new off-world home, while extraterrestrial landmarks like Orion take center stage in Roy Batty's (Rutger Hauer) iconic "tears in rain" monologue. Neither the Blade Runner films nor the animated series Blade Runner: Black Lotus have ever left Earth.

In a recent development, that all changes with Blade Runner 2099's Namaka Moon opening. The sequence focuses not on what life in an off-world colony looks like, but rather the labor that goes into establishing one in the first place.

In the episode, replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) clambers across the moon's rocky surface, establishing a series of beacons that shoot beams of light into Namaka's cloudy atmosphere. Once she leaves the moon, the beacons detonate in a series of spectacular explosions, presumably the first step in Namaka's terraforming process. As she tells companion replicant Marek (Johnny Harris), Namaka will be ready for human habitation in 20 years' time thanks to her work. Fittingly, the episode is titled "Birther of Worlds.".

Industry observers note that the Namaka sequence does a spectacular job of ushering Blade Runner into its own Space Age. But it isn't just a trip to space for space's sake. The entire episode opening is rooted in the replicant experience: the loneliness of traversing a perilous moon alone. The awe of watching a world come to life thanks to your handiwork. The hollowness of realizing you will never live in that world, nor be recognized for that work. It's key to understanding Olwen's character, as well as understanding the role of replicants in general. You could almost imagine Roy performing a similar task back in his day.

Sources indicate that plus, since Blade Runner 2099 has yet to show what an actual off-world colony might look like, it still leaves the door open for future Blade Runner projects to flesh out that aspect of the world onscreen. Clearly, the world is far, far vaster than just Los Angeles. Maybe Namaka is just the beginning.

UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
  • National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) mentioned it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses.
  • The NCSC indicates that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.

The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) mentioned it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.

The NCSC indicates that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.

The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.

While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.

“Notably, the problems being exploited presently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.

The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.

The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”.

The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that an Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.

    Recent findings suggest that the November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.

    “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.

    Amazon Prime Air at the moment operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case—so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.

    The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as “UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff.” That notice was posted on November 23.

    Sources indicate that the National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents.

    Logan Coomes, the neighbor whose garage was struck by the drone, described an Amazon Prime Air team arriving within 10 minutes and coordinating with Detroit Edison workers to eventually remove the drone by early evening, in an interview with WXYZ 7.

    Industry observers note that the Amazon Prime Air team also reportedly told Coomes that the company would help with repairs to his garage roof, and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card on the spot. Amazon claimed that this was the first such delivery drone crash from its operations near Detroit.

    It has been revealed that however, this would also add to the handful of Amazon drone incidents already under investigation by the US government. In October 2025, two Amazon delivery drones crashed into a construction crane in Tolleson, Arizona, while another delivery drone downed an Internet cable in Waco, Texas, the following month.

    The FAA has also been investigating an Amazon Prime Air drone crash involving an apartment building in Richardson, Texas, that occurred in February 2026.

    In response to the latest crash in Michigan, an Amazon spokesperson described Prime Air drones as making nearly 6,000 flights per day and already having delivered “hundreds of thousands of packages this year” in a statement shared with CNN.

    Amazon has been growing its Prime Air service with the goal of having delivery drones reach nearly 500 cities and towns across the United States by the end of 2026. The manufacturer has described delivery drones as enabling faster deliveries through potentially lower-emission and lower-cost operations compared with relying solely on ground vehicles.

    But the growth of delivery drone services has also drawn noise complaints from people living in neighborhoods where drones operate. As Sean Gallagher has written for Ars, the constant buzz of drones could even trigger post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders—especially for people who have directly or indirectly experienced some aspect of modern drone warfare.

    #116813. Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (657 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Is your Starlink Wi-Fi slower than it should be?
    • It has been revealed that while Starlink has had a lot of bad press in 2026 — mostly because of reported slowdowns in Ukraine and its general association with Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — there's no denying that for some people, it may be their best or only internet option.
    • There are a variety of ways Starlink can be optimized, an obvious one being dish placement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Is your Starlink Wi-Fi slower than it should be? A simple change in the app can help, though it comes with a few trade-offs worth knowing first.

    It has been revealed that while Starlink has had a lot of bad press in 2026 — mostly because of reported slowdowns in Ukraine and its general association with Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — there's no denying that for some people, it may be their best or only internet option. That's because Starlink satellites have wide global coverage, reaching areas inaccessible not just to landline connections but potentially competing cellular and satellite services as well.

    There are a variety of ways Starlink can be optimized, an obvious one being dish placement. Less obvious, though, is controlling how your system broadcasts Wi-Fi. You'd think the hard part would be capturing signals from space, after all, not bouncing them a few more feet to your laptop or TV.

    Sources indicate that what we're specifically talking about here is splitting your Wi-Fi into separate 2.4 and 5GHz networks in the Starlink app. We'll explain what that means, why it can be beneficial and when you may want to stick with the normal unified setting.

    If you already know why you'd want to split Wi-Fi, let's cut to the chase. All you have to do is find and select the Add Network option, then toggle Split Network. You'll be asked to name the two upcoming networks, which should probably include "2.4" and "5" so you can tell which network your devices are connecting to.

    For everyone else, it helps to know that most Wi-Fi routers are dual-band, broadcasting over two main frequency bands, 2.4 and 5GHz. Starlink's bundled hardware doesn't at the moment support the newer 6GHz band, even when it's equipped with Wi-Fi 7. The reason a split might help is that 5GHz is inherently faster than 2.4GHz. Shorter wavelengths translate not just into higher potential speeds but more non-overlapping channels. Overlap can result in congestion and interference. For devices that support 5GHz, then, forcing them to use the band all the time may result in noticeable speed boosts. As with any Wi-Fi network, exact performance figures are going to depend on a variety of factors, including not just your router but the range and kinds of devices connecting to your network.

    As if that weren't enough, some low-power devices, such as many Wi-Fi smart LED light bulbs, are 2.4GHz-only. If they're competing with devices that could be on 5GHz, they might be encountering unnecessary congestion of their own.

    The first potential issue here is range. The 2.4GHz band offers the greatest reach of any Wi-Fi band, typically up to 150 feet (45 meters) indoors, versus 5GHz's 50 to 75 feet (15 to 25 meters). It also offers better penetration through walls and other obstacles. In some scenarios, then, limiting devices to 5GHz may result in a flaky signal or none at all where things were previously stable. Under a unified network, devices can flip between bands automatically as needed.

    The other major concern is that devices on one network ID might not be able to talk to those on the other. They should be able to on paper, and naturally, that won't matter if all they have to do is communicate with the internet. But if you do encounter this matter, it can wreak havoc, particularly with a mix of smart home accessories that require specific bands. You may not be able to configure them all to work together, let alone trigger complex automations.

    In a recent development, one final problem is convenience. Reassigning a bunch of devices to latest networks can be a hassle, and to deal with range, you may have to manually switch some mobile devices every time you take them into a particular room. If you're not encountering any performance barriers with your existing setup, you might want to leave Starlink untouched.

    Industry News: Blade Runner 2099 sneaks in a book detail that never made it into the movies

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K.
    • Sources indicate that the 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants.
    • However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?

    Sources indicate that the 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants. Characters from the novel were cut, including Iran, the wife of Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford), and John Isidore, who houses the androids Deckard hunts. (William Sanderson's J.F. Sebastian effectively replaces him in the film.) These are just some world-building details from Dick's work that Blade Runner couldn't fit into a feature-length film.

    However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.

    Recent findings suggest that in Blade Runner 2099's sixth episode, replicants Julius (Tom Burke) and Clotilde (Amy Lennox) drive past a large billboard that advertises "the power of Mercer." The display is a reference to the fictional religion of Mercerism, built around the martyr Wilbur Mercer. Much of the rest of the episode takes place at the abandoned island Mercer Monastery where Cora (Hunter Schafer) grew up.

    It has been revealed that mercerism was initially conceptualized in Dick's 1964 short story "The Little Black Box." Followers connect with Mercer by gripping the handles of an empathy box. This device allows the user to experience Mercer's climb to his death: a slow ascent up a hill during which he's stoned repeatedly.

    According to recent reports, dick revisits Mercerism in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, in which Deckard uses an empathy box and sees visions of Mercer. However, radio host Buster Friendly exposes that the Mercer seen in the empathy boxes is simply a character played by an actor. Buster is omitted from Blade Runner and its sequel Blade Runner 2049. In Blade Runner 2099, however, he is played by Hugo Hamlet, and can be spotted in TV broadcasts.

    Mercer plays a key role in Blade Runner 2099 episode 6, which is named "Kill the Killers" after Mercer's major tenet: "You shall kill only the killers.".

    When Cora and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) investigate the monastery,  they encounter the lone Mercerite (David Dencik) living there. He's keeping up a religious telecast devoted to Mercer, and he claims the signal is strong enough to reach Los Angeles. But given that no one else has joined him, it appears his efforts are just shouting into the void.

    Recent findings suggest that the Mercerite has an empathy box, and he prompts Olwen to use it while he holds her at gunpoint. Within, she sees Mercer (Tomas Rydval) making his last climb. As unseen forces pelt him with rocks, the empathy box shocks Olwen's hands to mimic the painful experience.

    Olwen eventually uses a loose handle from the box to stab her captor. Then, she and Cora escape the island without becoming Mercer converts. (Sorry, Wilbur.).

    The episode functions both as a tribute to this piece of world-building and as a key subplot that was initially lost when Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? leaped from page to screen.

    Buster Friendly and Wilbur Mercer may not have gotten their time to shine in Blade Runner or Blade Runner 2049, but in a TV series like Blade Runner 2099, there is space to expand on the world and give them a moment in the spotlight, no matter how brief.

    Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

    A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.

    Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.

    Industry observers note that the group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.

    Sources indicate that they were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.

    Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.

    The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is noted to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.

    Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.

    Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.

    His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.

    Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.

    In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.

    In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.

    He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • According to recent reports, australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, the Associated Press reports, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021 that would set minimum safety standards for online platforms and provide ways to fine tech companies that don't comply.
    • Sources indicate that if passed, the Digital Duty of Care Bill would require online platforms and services like games, social media apps and AI chatbots to protect Australians from harmful content and conduct, according to the AP, including protecting children from exposure to content that promotes eating disorders and pornography.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The amendment would give the country a similar ability to fine tech companies as the EU’s Digital Services Act from 2022.

    According to recent reports, australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, the Associated Press reports, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021 that would set minimum safety standards for online platforms and provide ways to fine tech companies that don't comply. The bill follows Australia's recent social media ban for children under 16, an attempt to protect younger internet consumers with limited success so far.

    Sources indicate that if passed, the Digital Duty of Care Bill would require online platforms and services like games, social media apps and AI chatbots to protect Australians from harmful content and conduct, according to the AP, including protecting children from exposure to content that promotes eating disorders and pornography. It would also guarantee users the ability to opt out of algorithmic feeds and empower the country's eSafety Commissioner to remove "nudify" websites and apps that use AI to generate and spread nonconsensual nude images. As with the European Union's Digital Services Act, the bill's real teeth come from its possible fines. In this case, Australian regulators could fine tech companies up to five percent of their global revenue, a cap that was raised this week from 109 million AUD, or about $72 million in the US, to help the bill pass the Senate.

    "Vaguely defined 'harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech," US Ambassador to Australia David Brat posted on X. "As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.".

    Recent findings suggest that similar concerns have been raised about the UK's Online Safety Act, which also applies safety standards to online platforms, and helped encourage a wave of upcoming age verification systems across US apps and services in the last year. The Wikimedia Foundation, the owner of Wikipedia, has challenged the ways the UK's law categorizes platforms as one example of how these laws can be ill-defined or overly broad. Australia's bill is expected to clear Parliament and become law by the end of the week, according to the AP.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics.
    • The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
    • At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the newly introduced treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics.

    The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

    At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the newly introduced treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

    In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing.

    There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

    On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

    Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

    He remarked the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

    "Those days are done, gone," Wale said.

    Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

    "Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity.".

    "We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions.".

    On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

    "There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo mentioned.

    The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

    It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

    Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

    "That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

    William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, noted the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

    Under the newly introduced treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

    Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

    The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

    Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (Â£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

    Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese remarked the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China.

    The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can get a manual from iFixit for free to guide you through the process.
    • According to recent reports, after a brief period of people worrying that Google that was abandoning Fitbit devices in favor of the Pixel Watch, the tech giant recently assuaged those fears by releasing two fresh devices, led by the Fitbit Edge.
    • An enhancement that might've caught your attention is the product's user-replaceable battery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can get a manual from iFixit for free to guide you through the process.

    According to recent reports, after a brief period of people worrying that Google that was abandoning Fitbit devices in favor of the Pixel Watch, the tech giant recently assuaged those fears by releasing two fresh devices, led by the Fitbit Edge. It's an obvious successor to the Charge series, albeit without Google Pay, or EDA scans for measuring stress.

    An enhancement that might've caught your attention is the product's user-replaceable battery. The dirty secret of most fitness trackers (and smartwatches, for that matter) is that while they can last for years, if their batteries aren't replaced, their capacity will inevitably shrink until it becomes unusable. In theory, as long Google maintains app support and compatible batteries are still in warehouses, an Edge can last indefinitely.

    It has been revealed that this isn't quite like replacing the AAs in a flashlight, however, or even the coin battery you might find in an analog watch. You need specialized gear, and the process is delicate enough that there's a risk of sabotaging your Fitbit if you make a mistake.

    Google's partner on this is iFixit, which provides a free PDF manual once you've signed into their website. Before you begin, however, you need to buy specialized parts and tools, including not just a fresh battery, but replacement screws for the surrounding equipment. That might seem strange, but iFixit says that these replacement parts can only be used once, a claim which may or may not say anything about the original parts as well.

    According to recent reports, where things get risky is after you've managed to pry open the Edge's case. Its O-ring can fall out, and you'll need to reassemble that if you want your device to retain any water resistance. You'll also need a pair of tweezers, and needless to say, poking circuits could accidentally break something, as could static shock. iFixit recommends precautions like a grounding mat, and even avoiding any clothing that could build up a static charge, such as fleece.

    In a recent development, for some owners, the major hurdle is going to be the scale of the operation. The screws and connectors involved are tiny, even by the standards of most electronics. If your hands aren't steady, this process could prove frustrating or outright impossible, speaking as someone who's hand-assembled desktop PCs.

    Officially, no. If you don't want to perform the procedure yourself, Google doesn't offer a paid replacement service. The manufacturer might conceivably perform a free swap if you've got a defective battery and you're still under warranty, but you're otherwise expected to handle things yourself. If you do qualify for a battery fix, there's a chance that Google will simply send you a replacement Edge.

    As time goes on, third-party options might arrive, yet Google cautions against using unofficial parts, stating that "a non-qualified battery and improper disposal may present a risk of fire, explosion, leakage, and/or other hazards." The organization is, of course, covering itself legally — but there's a grain of truth in that there's no telling what the quality of a generic part may be. Lithium-ion batteries can burst into flames if they're damaged or defective. Even with Google's official parts, you should be prepared to dispose of a battery in a fireproof container.

    Recent findings suggest that all this helps to explain why more wearables haven't gone the replaceable route. Companies don't want to be on the hook for their customers' mistakes, and it remains to be seen how many people will actually take advantage of the option. By the time an Edge's battery wears out, you might be more inclined to buy a newer device than resuscitate last-gen hardware.

    Back-to-back measles deaths is our latest reality; US tally now at 14

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic.
    • Industry observers note that the national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991.
    • On November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department unveiled its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

    Industry observers note that the national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

    On November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department unveiled its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. Fresh York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.

    According to recent reports, the virus isn’t slowing down. Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in the air for up to two hours. Up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will fall ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they’ve been vaccinated or previously infected. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible people is only growing.

    To keep measles from getting a foothold in a community, vaccination rates need to be 95 percent or higher. According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. But even in those states, there are pockets and communities that are undervaccinated.

    In Pennsylvania, which has the record for the largest measles outbreak this year so far, the epidemic curve appears to be past the peak. But Wisconsin seems to be in the thick of its outbreak. As of today, the state case count hit 920, with 88 cases reported since November 20. The health department has tallied 418 cases since the start of the month.

    In most cases, measles causes high fever, a telltale rash, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. But some develop complications, which can be severe and even life-threatening, including pneumonia and brain swelling, which can result in intellectual disabilities and hearing loss. In pregnant people, measles can cause more severe illness and pregnancy complications, including premature birth, low birth weight, and congenital measles.

    After an acute infection, every person infected faces a long immune recovery in which they are newly vulnerable to a slew of other diseases. The measles virus specifically infects and destroys memory immune cells, which hold molecular records of germs the immune system has previously encountered and defeated. In other words, the immunity built up over the person’s life gets wiped, a phenomenon called immune amnesia. A study in 2019 estimated that the measles virus erases up to 73 percent of a person’s antibody repertoire, which would otherwise defend against infections and reinfections. To regain protection, people must be exposed to the germs again, either through reinfections or repeat vaccinations.

    People who appear to recover are also at risk of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare but devastating condition in which the virus remains in the central nervous system, striking years later to cause a progressive, fatal neurological disease.

    #116796. Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (898 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis.
    • The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
    • Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

    The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

    Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

    The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

    To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

    However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

    These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of latest proportions.

    Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace.".

    "This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," stated Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

    "We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

    Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing.".

    He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

    "Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," remarked Mgbeahuruike.

    Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

    He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

    Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

    Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

    Industry observers note that ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

    However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

    Recent findings suggest that voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

    Breaking: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal.
    • South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
    • Sources indicate that in 2022, an independent panel stated Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal.

    South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.

    Sources indicate that in 2022, an independent panel stated Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (Â£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.

    Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.

    The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety".

    In its judgment, the court stated the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make".

    "It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana remarked.

    The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report.

    Political analyst Khanyi Magubane stated the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility".

    She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report.

    "[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane noted.

    The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.

    The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.

    Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.

    The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.

    Opposition parties, pictured above, have been vocal in their call for the president to account for his role in the saga.

    Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.

    Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but stated the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.

    Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.

    The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".

    It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".

    Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.

    He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.

    It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.

    In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".

    The Western Cape High Court's ruling could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.

    If they do, and the appeal is successful, the parliamentary committee would be able to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.

    If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.

    Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.

    He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

    Legal expert Professor Richard Calland told the BBC he had expected the court ruling, given what he termed as "fault lines" in the independent panel's report.

    Calland stated the court's findings now meant that the impeachment process was "dead in the water [and] cannot continue".

    He mentioned that any political party that wanted to revive it "would have to come up with a whole newly introduced basis" for this.

    Calland said political parties who want to hold Ramaphosa accountable would likely seek to appeal the ruling but it was unlikely parliament would also do so.

    "So, the president's political career is now free of the cloud of impeachment," he stated.

    Latest Update: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that as AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing.
    • Recent findings suggest that “We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman.
    • “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that as AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple, co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the organization itself.

    Recent findings suggest that “We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman. “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.”.

    “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.

    The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies and data collection practices, and sometimes even training on users’ personal data.

    Instead of asking owners to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.

    It has been revealed that like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly rolled out desktop app, Maple Work, offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.

    In a recent development, with the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and other AI agents that work over chat.

    Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.

    According to recent reports, at Apple, he worked on AI and machine learning with a particular focus on computer vision. Given Apple’s stance on consumer privacy, the challenge he faced was building products that would protect people’s identity while benefiting from computer vision techniques. His co-founder, Anthony Ronning (CTO), has a background in defense tech, security, and networking.

    It has been revealed that ronning started the company that later became Maple AI back in 2023, initially as a privacy-focused fintech. When Suman teamed up with Ronning in August 2024, the idea to create Maple AI was born. The following January, the product became available to the public as a mobile app.

    According to recent reports, the app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma, and OpenAI’s GPT OSS. Customers can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one.

    The models themselves run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe.).

    Sources indicate that “We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it. It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there. The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds.

    This allows Maple to protect its consumers’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance. All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file.

    “We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model. And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.”.

    Sources indicate that with the new desktop app, Maple is looking to small businesses that may want to benefit from AI without the data privacy risks. Inside the app, there’s an integration store where users can connect with other apps, like their Gmail or calendar. The desktop app can also spin up a subagent that works inside another AI app you may have on your desktop, like Claude, Codex, or others that support the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). This allows customers to use their preferred AI app for specific tasks, without having to give it all their information — just what’s needed for the given task.

    Recent findings suggest that next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion.

    The company declined to share its registered customer numbers but noted it’s seen 60x growth over the past three months, as people have been looking for ways to increase their security with AI.

    Maple currently generates revenue via subscriptions, which are comparable to those from other AI model providers. Its Pro strategy is $20 per month, and it offers two Max plans, Max and Max Plus, at $100 and $200 per month, respectively.

    The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup is a team of four and is actively hiring.

    #116788. You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (645 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.
    • Industry observers note that one of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities.
    • Recent findings suggest that one way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.

    Industry observers note that one of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.

    Recent findings suggest that one way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.

    In a recent development, here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.

    According to recent reports, to enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.

    Industry observers note that that last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.

    The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.

    When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.

    According to recent reports, the honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.

    Industry observers note that the main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.

    Industry observers note that if your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

    #116784. Breaking: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1172 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
    • It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

    It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

    Recent findings suggest that the Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”.

    The proof of the hypothesis was declared by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

    In a recent development, but it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

    The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

    It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

    But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

    It has been revealed that AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

    The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

    It has been revealed that mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

    Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

    Industry observers note that but that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever concerns they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less key for math than the process of generating it.

    Industry observers note that by contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of newly introduced ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.

    Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce upcoming insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

    How mathematicians are expected to identify fresh challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

    Industry observers note that this is all newly introduced and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.

    But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some drivers swear by this Apple Watch feature, and it's probably already switched on.

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    It has been revealed that if you're deep into the Apple ecosystem, the choice between Apple Maps and Google Maps isn't as clear-cut as it used to be. The first was initially a disaster, even threatening the lives of Australian drivers due to inaccuracies. Since then, however, Apple has totally overhauled the app, and these days there's often little to no practical difference — speaking as someone who recently drove cross-country to move to a new city.

    I did prefer Apple Maps for that drive for one big reason: my Apple Watch. I knew that I'd be driving for hours at a time, and it was essential to exploit anything and everything to stay alert. Linked with CarPlay, the Apple Watch offers a distinct advantage in the form of haptic feedback.

    Sources indicate that most likely this option will already be on once you've configured your watch. But you can double-check this on your iPhone and turn off the feature if it becomes more of an annoyance than a benefit.

    Recent findings suggest that with haptic feedback active, your Apple Watch taps your wrist whenever a turn is imminent. These vibrations coincide with CarPlay's audio and visual alerts, so it's always clear what you're supposed to do. You can even choose different vibration patterns depending on whether you need to turn left or right. This makes it virtually impossible to miss a turnoff; the feature might even be lifesaving if you're prone to nodding off on long drives.

    As mentioned, these alerts should be on by default. If you want to verify that or disable them, open the Watch app on your iPhone. On the My Watch tab, select Apps, then Maps. If you like, you can toggle alerts for Driving with CarPlay, plus any other driving, walking or cycling.

    Whether or not you disable CarPlay integration, you'll probably want to leave cycling alerts on. Apple Maps can be handy while riding a bike or a personal electric vehicle such as a scooter or electric unicycle, but it's sometimes difficult to check your screen and ride at the same time. Audio and haptics may be your only practical cues to make a turn.

    According to recent reports, unfortunately, it's impossible to run CarPlay exclusively from your Apple Watch. Even the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lacks the necessary horsepower, and CarPlay would be an immense battery drain regardless. Since Apple Watches also lack USB ports, they'd be restricted to wireless CarPlay at best.

    Recent findings suggest that you can get driving directions directly from the watchOS version of Apple Maps. You'll get the same sort of haptics we've been talking about, plus audio and visual guidance. If you don't have your iPhone, you'll need to download offline maps or use a watch with an active cellular plan. Many carriers charge extra for smartwatch coverage, even though you're rarely going to use your watch and phone data at the same time.

    While you can get Google Maps on an Apple Watch, directions won't work without your iPhone. There's no watchOS option for offline maps, and Apple Watches are largely restricted to first-party apps while on cellular. These issues may be solved someday, but neither Apple nor Google seems that eager to tackle them.

    Industry News: Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (377 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.
    • If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode.
    • Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.

    If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.

    Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.

    Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.

    There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.

    Industry observers note that in your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.

    It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials mentioned.

    Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

    Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he remarked.

    Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, remarked: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families.".
